events.text:
🇺🇦 ⚠️ 🇺🇸 #Musk Asked #Trump To Slow Down #Ukraine's Military Defenses, Telegraph Exclusive Reveals: 
Elon Musk approached Donald Trump with the idea of slowing down Starlink in Ukraine, The Telegraph can reveal.
The billionaire tech entrepreneur approached the US president with the proposal to introduce speed limits on the system, which hampered Ukraine’s drone defences, according to four sources familiar with the discussions
One of the sources said Mr Trump “agreed” with Mr Musk’s suggestion, paving the way for the Pentagon to execute the slowdown on Starshield.
Mr Musk had previously blamed Mr Trump for the chaos, claiming any changes would have been decided by the US military and ultimately the president.
At the time, Mr Trump was embroiled in a row with Volodymyr Zelensky over Ukraine’s strikes on Russian oil refineries.
US officials had warned Kyiv’s team of peace negotiators that the U.S. could shut off intelligence-sharing and other kinds of support if the long-range attacks were not halted. 
Earlier this week, one of Mr Zelensky’s advisers said Mr Musk’s SpaceX had restricted access to the Starshield system, used by Kyiv to intercept jet-powered drones and strike behind enemy lines.
Speaking on the fringes of an EU summit on Friday, the Ukrainian president called the slowdown a “very dangerous and unpleasant surprise”.
Mr Musk denied he was responsible for limiting Starlink access, blaming the White House. He claimed that “any limits on speed or usage” were “decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS”, referring to Mr Trump.
However, after what was described as a “night of carnage” in Kyiv because of the blackout, a senior source said Mr Musk had been alarmed about the possibility of adverse consumer reaction in Europe.
The source said: “He tweeted out that he was innocent and that it was the US administration that did it. The reality is that they were both in it.”
A high-ranking European official and two well-placed Ukrainian sources confirmed this version of events.
Speaking on Friday evening, Mr Trump said he did not think ‌either ‌he ⁠nor Mr Musk had been responsible for Ukraine ⁠losing Starlink access.
On Friday, an anonymous US official, cited in a report by the AFP, insisted that Trump did not make the request for a reduction of Starshield’s services for Ukraine. “No request was ever made by the president,” the US official said, after a report by Reuters claimed the decision came from the White House. 
The Pentagon has not publicly explained the restrictions.
The speed cap imposed on Ukraine limited drones using the Starshield system to around 160kmph, making it virtually impossible to intercept Russia’s barrages of jet-powered drones and missiles, which travel double the speed.
On Friday, Mr Zelensky said signals were being restored.
It is not the first time Mr Musk has been accused of limiting the use of his Starlink platform to the detriment of Ukraine.
In 2023, he confirmed he had rebutted requests by Kyiv to use the system in drone attacks on Crimea, the peninsula illegally annexed by Russia, to avoid being complicit in a “major act of war”.
Mr Musk was lauded by Ukrainians earlier this year for his direct role in blocking illegal access to Starlink by Russian soldiers fighting in Ukraine.
Radek Sikorski, Poland’s foreign minister, warned the tech billionaire: “As your European customers, we are watching you.”
The EU is planning to have its Iris2, a Starlink replacement, operational by 2030. Mr Zelensky arrived in Brussels bruised and seeking more support from his European allies after his war of words with Mr Trump.
Diplomats said leaders had advised the Ukrainian president to tone down his criticism of his US counterpart amid fears Washington could further withdraw its support for Kyiv.
Mr Trump has been highly critical of Ukraine’s strikes on Russia’s oil refineries, blaming them for soaring energy prices before the midterm elections next month.
More: www.telegraph.co.uk/world-news/2026/10/16/musk-approached-trump-slow-down-starlink-help-ukraine/

events.text:
Romania resumed its search Friday for seven sailors missing from the San Marino flagged chemical tanker "Wine Trader", which was hit by a drone early Thursday in the Black Sea, Reuters reports. The ship was about a mile outside Romanian territorial waters. Twelve sailors were aboard, five were rescued, and strong winds and rough seas hampered the search.
An interior ministry spokesperson said rescuers returned to search the ship. A Black Hawk helicopter would place four rescuers aboard while another ship searched nearby waters.
A second tanker, the Comoros flagged "Yara J", was hit by a drone inside Romanian waters late Wednesday. Its crew was unharmed and it was towed to the port of Constanta. Both ships were anchored near the Sulina canal, which links the Danube to the Black Sea and is a key export route for Ukraine, Reuters reports.
Romanian President Nicusor Dan said drones struck both ships. A NATO military source told Reuters the drones came from Russia.
Reuters says at least five other cargo ships were hit near Romania and Bulgaria in the past 10 days, with 23 sailors dead or missing. Most of those incidents were outside NATO territorial waters.
Source: https://www.reuters.com/world/romania-resumes-search-seven-missing-sailors-drone-hit-ship-2026-10-16/

🪖 Erik Prince’s costly mercenary force fails to deliver on Haiti’s security promises 
Blackwater founder Erik Prince, who made his fortune offering security services worldwide, often outside the law,[ has been selling ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/64481)Haiti a high-tech mercenary solution to its gang crisis, but the country remains trapped in violence, reports CNN.
Prince’s private force, Vectus Global, was hired by Haiti’s interim government last year[ for a mission to hunt gangs.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/55395)
His task force paired foreign contractors with elite local police to unleash more than 2,000 drone strikes since March last year. 
While some gang positions have reportedly been disrupted, the promised turnaround has not arrived.
➡️ vital road from Cap-Haitien to Port-au-Prince still sits under gang checkpoints more than 18 months after Prince said it would be freed within a year
➡️ international flights remain grounded for risk of being shot down over gang territory
➡️ general elections, once set for December, have been postponed indefinitely
➡️ gangs have simply shifted outward into farming communities that feed the country
➡️ forcible recruitment of children has tripled, with minors now making up 30–50 % of many groups
➡️ civilian casualties from the drone campaign stand at least at 85 dead according to UN tallies
➡️ over 1.5 million Haitians - roughly one-tenth of the population - remain internally displaced
Local human-rights advocates describe the expensive foreign presence as largely ineffective: no major gang leaders have been eliminated, armed groups still flaunt weapons and money online.
Prince refuses to name his fee, only claiming it is a fraction of earlier multinational missions, while securing a decade-long deal for a cut of future border customs revenue.

🇺🇸🇮🇷 Price of war: How US aggression against Iran bleeds global oil markets dry
Eight months into the Iran conflict, the global oil market is being reshaped by disruptions at two chokepoints that together carry a huge share of global crude. The Strait of Hormuz has been the primary battleground, while the Bab al-Mandeb has now emerged as a second front, CNN reports.
🔶 Iran has recently stepped up strikes on tankers trying to pass through Hormuz and [the Persian Gulf,](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76299) pushing crude prices above $100 a barrel 
🔶 The strikes come amid a US shuttle system in which tankers sail with transponders switched off, transferring cargo to ships waiting in the Gulf of Oman. The White House uses the system to ease [the pressure on oil markets ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75696)
Meanwhile, fighting between Saudi Arabia and Houthi forces in Yemen has turned the Red Sea route into a new pressure point. The Houthis have targeted Saudi oil tankers transiting Bab al-Mandeb and launched strikes on Riyadh's main international airport.
➡️ Before the hostilities escalated this summer, the Saudi Red Sea port of Yanbu exported around 4.5 million barrels per day at its peak, with roughly 3 million of that leaving through Bab al-Mandeb.
➡️ By June, daily loadings from Yanbu had fallen 41% to about 2.39 million barrels, and as of mid-October flows through the strait stood at roughly 1.5 million barrels per day — about half the pre-war level
➡️ After drone attacks from inside Iraq struck [the East-West pipeline](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75123) that feeds Saudi Arabia's Red Sea terminals last month, Saudi Arabia moved quickly to redirect exports back through Hormuz, relying on the US-assisted shuttle operation
The Saudi-led coalition launched a large-scale counteroffensive against the Houthis in early October to counter the threat to oil flows. But those gains have proved fragile. Houthi forces repelled subsequent advances, inflicting heavy casualties and destroying armored vehicles,[ according to reports](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76209). The Houthis have consolidated control over thousands of square kilometers along the western coast, including the stretch from Mocha to Bab al-Mandeb, and continue [to besiege Taiz](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76352), cutting the city's supply routes.
